# When a CA Is Distrusted: Go 1.27.3's x509 Denylist and Rebuilding Binaries

After this page you will know where Go's fix for a distrusted certificate authority (CA) lives, why updating the operating system's CA bundle does not fix a Go binary, how to build with a patched toolchain without reinstalling Go, and how to find the binaries that still need rebuilding.

## What happened: The eMudhra incident

In October 2026, eight eMudhra (emSign) intermediate CA certificates were found to have trivially weak private keys: every one of the eight elliptic-curve private keys was a number below 256. A key that small can be found by simply trying every value, so anyone could issue certificates that chain up to roots that clients already trust.

The CA revoked the certificates. Revocation only helps clients that check it, though, and Go's `crypto/x509` does not check CRLs or OCSP during chain verification. Go shipped its fix on 19–20 October 2026, the first release on Go's URGENT security track.

The emergency updates—Go 1.27.3 and Go 1.26.10—addressed the issue tracked as CVE-2026-111943, Go vulnerability ID GO-2026-6809 ("Distrust compromised intermediate certificates in crypto/x509"), and upstream issue go.dev/issue/82345.

The fix is code in `crypto/x509`, so it is compiled into every binary built with a fixed toolchain, and only into those binaries.

## Why Go's fix lives in your binary

Go's standard library package `crypto/x509` performs TLS certificate chain validation. In Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10, the Go team added a hardcoded denylist containing the SHA-256 cryptographic hashes of the `RawSubjectPublicKeyInfo` bytes for the eight compromised intermediate keys.

During certificate chain construction in `crypto/x509`, any candidate certificate chain containing one of these compromised public keys is discarded. This protection applies universally:

1. **Every platform**: on macOS and Windows, Go normally hands verification to the platform verifier, and the denylist applies there too.
2. **Cross-signing protection**: Because the denylist matches against the `RawSubjectPublicKeyInfo` hash rather than the certificate signature or subject name, cross-signed variants of the same intermediate keys (such as those signed via Sectigo AAA Certificate Services) are rejected as well.
3. **No runtime opt-out**: There is intentionally no `GODEBUG` environment variable to disable this denylist.

Crucially, because this logic is embedded directly inside the `crypto/x509` package code during compilation, upgrading the operating system's CA bundle on a server does **not** protect existing Go binaries. Similarly, upgrading the Go toolchain on a build host does not protect production services until every binary is explicitly recompiled and redeployed.

| Action | Protects Go Binaries Built Prior to Patch? | Protects Non-Go System Tools? | Requires Binary Recompilation? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **OS CA Bundle Update** | No | Yes | No |
| **Upgrade Go on Build Host** | No (until rebuild) | No | No |
| **Rebuild Binary with Go 1.27.3 / 1.26.10** | Yes | No | Yes |

Conversely, once a binary is recompiled with Go 1.27.3 or 1.26.10, it remains protected against the compromised keys even if deployed onto an older, unpatched host operating system whose system root store still trusts the emSign root.

## What the failure looks like

When a binary built with a fixed toolchain meets a server whose chain needs one of the distrusted keys, chain building fails.

The underlying error is an `x509.CertificateInvalidError` with `Reason` set to `x509.NoValidChains`, which `http.Get` or `tls.Dial` wraps in its own error. In logs it ends with:

```text
x509: no valid chains built
```

Because all candidate chains containing the compromised key material are filtered out, `Verify` behaves as though no valid path to a trusted root could be found.

## Rebuilding your Go applications

To protect your applications, every Go binary that performs outbound HTTPS requests, connects to TLS-protected databases, or validates client TLS certificates must be recompiled using Go 1.27.3 (or Go 1.26.10 for the Go 1.26 release line).

Since Go 1.21, Go features native toolchain management via the `GOTOOLCHAIN` environment variable and the `toolchain` directive in `go.mod`. You do not need to manually reinstall Go across developer workstations or build environments to target a newer patch release.

### Setting toolchain explicitly in `go.mod`

The demo module's `go.mod` (in `fetch/`) is as small as it gets:

<!-- file: fetch/go.mod -->
```text
module example.com/fetch

go 1.27
```

To make every build of the module use at least the fixed toolchain, add a `toolchain` line below `go 1.27`:

```text
toolchain go1.27.3
```

With the default `GOTOOLCHAIN=auto`, an older `go` command that meets this line downloads and runs Go 1.27.3 instead. For a one-off build, set `GOTOOLCHAIN` directly, as shown below.

### Demonstration binary

`fetch/main.go` fetches an HTTPS URL and prints how many verified chains the TLS handshake produced:

<!-- file: fetch/main.go -->
```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"net/http"
	"os"
)

func main() {
	url := "https://go.dev/"
	if len(os.Args) > 1 {
		url = os.Args[1]
	}
	resp, err := http.Get(url)
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Println("error:", err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	defer resp.Body.Close()
	fmt.Println(resp.Status, "verified chain(s):", len(resp.TLS.VerifiedChains))
}
```

### Using `GOTOOLCHAIN` at build time

You can instruct Go to automatically download and execute Go 1.27.3 without modifying the system Go installation by setting `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.3`.

Check which toolchain that selects:

```bash
GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.3 go version
```

The following command produced this output:
```text
go version go1.27.3 linux/amd64
```

The system Go on this machine is 1.27.2. Build the program twice, once with it and once with 1.27.3, then ask each binary what built it:

```bash
cd fetch
go build -o ../bin/fetch-1.27.2 .
GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.3 go build -o ../bin/fetch-1.27.3 .
cd ..
go version bin/fetch-1.27.2 bin/fetch-1.27.3
```

The following command produced this output:
```text
bin/fetch-1.27.2: go1.27.2
bin/fetch-1.27.3: go1.27.3
```

`go version FILE...` reads the build information embedded in each binary, so it tells you which toolchain built it without access to the source code.

An ordinary site still verifies with the fixed binary:

```bash
./bin/fetch-1.27.3
```

The following command produced this output:
```text
200 OK verified chain(s): 2
```

### Updating CI build environments

Pin CI build images to a Go 1.27.3 (or 1.26.10) tag or later, not just a floating `1.27`, and confirm what was actually used by running `go version` on the artifact. Where you can't change the image, the `toolchain go1.27.3` line in `go.mod` (with `GOTOOLCHAIN=auto`) or an explicit `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.3` in the build script gets the fixed toolchain, as long as the build can reach the module proxy to download it.

## Finding old binaries in your environment

Go binaries carry their build information, so you can audit binaries in images, artifacts and servers without the source.

### Using `go version` and `debug/buildinfo`

`go version` accepts any number of files and skips anything that isn't a Go binary:

```bash
go version /usr/local/bin/*
```

For automated inventory auditing, Go provides the standard library package `debug/buildinfo`. You can write a scanner tool that walks directory trees and flags any binary compiled with an unpatched Go version.

Below is the module configuration for a build scanner tool:

<!-- file: gobinscan/go.mod -->
```text
module example.com/gobinscan

go 1.27

require golang.org/x/mod v0.42.0
```

Below is the implementation of `gobinscan`, which inspects Go binaries and evaluates their release versions using `golang.org/x/mod/semver`:

<!-- file: gobinscan/main.go -->
```go
// gobinscan walks directories and reports Go binaries built with a
// toolchain older than the minimum you name for each release line.
package main

import (
	"debug/buildinfo"
	"fmt"
	"io/fs"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
	"strings"

	"golang.org/x/mod/semver"
)

// Minimum patched release per Go minor line (eMudhra distrust, Oct 2026).
var minimum = map[string]string{
	"v1.27": "v1.27.3",
	"v1.26": "v1.26.10",
}

func verdict(goVersion string) string {
	v := "v" + strings.TrimPrefix(goVersion, "go")
	v = strings.SplitN(v, " ", 2)[0] // drop " X:..." experiment suffixes
	if !semver.IsValid(v) {
		return "UNKNOWN"
	}
	need, ok := minimum[semver.MajorMinor(v)]
	if !ok {
		if semver.Compare(v, "v1.27.0") > 0 {
			return "ok"
		}
		return "UNSUPPORTED"
	}
	if semver.Compare(v, need) < 0 {
		return "REBUILD (needs " + strings.TrimPrefix(need, "v") + ")"
	}
	return "ok"
}

func main() {
	roots := os.Args[1:]
	if len(roots) == 0 {
		roots = []string{"."}
	}
	for _, root := range roots {
		filepath.WalkDir(root, func(path string, d fs.DirEntry, err error) error {
			if err != nil || d.IsDir() {
				return nil
			}
			info, err := buildinfo.ReadFile(path)
			if err != nil {
				return nil // not a Go binary
			}
			fmt.Printf("%-28s %-10s %s\n", path, info.GoVersion, verdict(info.GoVersion))
			return nil
		})
	}
}
```

Run `gobinscan` across your local binary directories:

```bash
./gobinscan bin /usr/local/bin
```

The following command produced this output:
```text
bin/fetch-1.27.2             go1.27.2   REBUILD (needs 1.27.3)
bin/fetch-1.27.3             go1.27.3   ok
/usr/local/bin/gh            go1.27.1   REBUILD (needs 1.27.3)
/usr/local/bin/go            go1.27.2   REBUILD (needs 1.27.3)
/usr/local/bin/gofmt         go1.27.2   REBUILD (needs 1.27.3)
```

Even the tools on the build machine show up: `gh`, `go` and `gofmt` were all built with older toolchains. A program that never verifies a TLS chain (`gofmt`, for example) is a lower priority than a network service, but the rule that scales is simple: rebuild everything you ship.

### Using `govulncheck` in binary mode

The official Go vulnerability scanner, `govulncheck`, supports analyzing compiled Go binaries directly. `govulncheck -mode=binary` goes beyond the version string: it looks at the symbols compiled into the binary and reports a vulnerability only if a vulnerable function, here `x509.Certificate.Verify` (reached through `net/http`), is present.

Install `govulncheck`:

```bash
go install golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest
```

Scan the unpatched binary built with Go 1.27.2:

```bash
govulncheck -mode=binary bin/fetch-1.27.2
```

The following command produced this output:
```text
=== Symbol Results ===

Vulnerability #1: GO-2026-6809
    Distrust compromised intermediate certificates in crypto/x509
  More info: https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-6809
  Standard library
    Found in: crypto/x509@go1.27.2
    Fixed in: crypto/x509@go1.27.3
    Vulnerable symbols found:
      #1: x509.Certificate.Verify

Your code is affected by 1 vulnerability from the Go standard library.
This scan found no other vulnerabilities in packages you import or modules you
require.
Use '-show verbose' for more details.
```

`govulncheck` identifies vulnerability GO-2026-6809 and exits with code 3 when vulnerabilities are detected.

Next, scan the patched binary built with Go 1.27.3:

```bash
govulncheck -mode=binary bin/fetch-1.27.3
```

The following command produced this output:
```text
No vulnerabilities found.
```

When no vulnerabilities are found in the binary symbols, `govulncheck` exits with code 0.

## Fleet playbook checklist

When responding to standard library security patches that require binary recompilation, follow this structured remediation plan across your infrastructure:

1. **Audit binary inventory**:
   Run `govulncheck -mode=binary` or `debug/buildinfo` scanning scripts across production container registries, AMI disk images, and server deployments to build an inventory of affected binaries.
2. **Update build toolchains**:
   Set `toolchain go1.27.3` in project `go.mod` files or ensure CI/CD runner environments export `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.3`.
3. **Rebuild all application binaries**:
   Trigger clean builds of all microservices, background workers, and ingress proxies.
4. **Redeploy container images and host binaries**:
   Rolling-update production deployments. Ensure old container layers containing unpatched binaries are replaced.
5. **Verify deployed artifacts**:
   Run `govulncheck -mode=binary` on the final release artifacts inside the CD pipeline before pushing to production registries.
6. **Maintain base images**:
   Update base container images (e.g., `alpine`, `debian`, `distroless`) to ensure OS-level certificate stores and auxiliary runtime utilities are also up to date.

## Pitfalls

When managing standard library security fixes across complex deployments, avoid these common traps:

### Distroless and minimal container images
A distroless or `scratch` image is a good idea for other reasons, but swapping or updating the base image changes nothing here. The standard library is inside your executable, so only a rebuild helps. The denylist applies whichever root store the binary ends up using.

### Vendored or static third-party binaries
Third-party utilities included in build pipelines or container images (for example `kubectl`, `helm` or your own sidecars) carry their own compiled Go standard libraries. Updating your own application code will not patch these third-party tools. You must update vendor tools to release versions built by their maintainers using Go 1.27.3 or 1.26.10.

### Attempting to disable TLS validation
If a connection starts failing with `x509: no valid chains built` after a rebuild, the server is serving a distrusted chain. Fix the server's certificate. Setting `InsecureSkipVerify: true` in `tls.Config` to make the error go away turns off exactly the protection this release added, along with all other chain checks.

## Summary

* **Toolchain-level enforcement**: Go embeds x509 validation rules and CA denylists directly into compiled binaries via `crypto/x509`.
* **OS updates don't cover it**: neither a new OS CA bundle nor a new Go on the build host changes a binary that has already been built.
* **CVE-2026-111943 / GO-2026-6809**: Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 introduce hardcoded SHA-256 denylists targeting compromised eMudhra (emSign) intermediate keys.
* **Rebuild requirement**: Every Go binary making TLS connections or validating certificates must be recompiled using Go 1.27.3 or Go 1.26.10.
* **Binary inspection**: Use `go version`, `debug/buildinfo`, and `govulncheck -mode=binary` to audit compiled binaries for unpatched toolchain versions.
